title: Why Penedès tastes the way it does

lede.text: Penedès sits in a young basin ringed by older mountains, under a Mediterranean climate. The growers' work, on this soil and in this climate, brings its white grapes to full ripeness.

chapters.title: A sunken basin between mountains
paras: The relief has three units. The Garraf massif and the pre-coastal range between Montserrat and the Montmell surround the Penedès pre-coastal depression. The oldest ground is in these mountain chains.

The depression itself is very young in geological terms. Long ago, before the Miocene age, the Garraf and the pre-coastal range were one unit. After the depression sank, recent erosion by rivers and torrents sharpened the relief at its edges and carved deep ravines in the north of the area.
The production zone is made up of municipalities in two provinces, Barcelona and Tarragona. Ten smaller named areas, such as Massís del Garraf or Costers del Montmell, may be added to a label.

chapters.title: A Mediterranean climate with a day-night gap
paras: Penedès has a Mediterranean climate. In July and August the temperature differs between night and day.
Climate and soil, helped by that gap, allow red grapes to ripen well. They come out rich in colour and tannins, and in red-fruit aromas.

chapters.title: Loamy soils that mostly drain well
paras: Active limestone, the fine and reactive part of the lime, runs between 5 and 10%. Soils are 40 cm to 120 cm or more deep, and most are between 80 and 120 cm. Drainage is generally good.
The surface texture is loam and silty loam. Between 1% and 5% of the soil at root depth is coarse stones.
A soil map decides which plots suit which grape.

chapters.title: Fresh whites, sparkling and sweet wines
paras: Penedès whites are known for their freshness, acidity and fruit, which come from this soil and climate and from the growers' work. Eighteen white varieties can go into the wine, Xarel·lo and Parellada among them. Ull de Llebre and Monastrell are among the 13 red varieties.
From the 2025 harvest on, all grapes and wines must be certified organic. Yields are capped at 12,000 kg per hectare for white varieties and sparkling wine, and 9,000 kg for red varieties.
Still wines are white, rosado (rosé) or red, at 9.5% vol. or more for white and rosado and 11% vol. for red. Rosados owe their colour, aroma and fruit to their grapes, grown in this soil and climate.

Sparkling wine is made by the traditional method, with at least 15 months from tirage, the bottling for the second fermentation, to disgorging, when the spent yeast is taken out, and a pressure of over 3.5 bar. It may also be made by the ancestral method, where the first fermentation is slowed or stopped so the grapes' own sugar drives the second, with no sugar or must added. By sugar it is labelled in seven steps, from Brut natural, under 3 g/l, to Dulce, over 50 g/l. Vino de aguja is a lightly sparkling wine, with a pressure of 1 to 2.5 bar.

Sweet wines come in four kinds. Vino dulce natural is a fortified wine made from overripe grapes of at least 240 g/l sugar, with alcohol added. Vino dulce de Malvasía de Sitges is also fortified, and is made only from the Malvasía de Sitges grape. Vino dulce de uva sobremadurada (overripe-grape sweet wine) is not fortified: it is made from overripe grapes with no artificial boost to strength. The fourth is the dulce de frío, in which cold stops fermentation and 70 to 150 g/l of sugar stays in the wine, with nothing added.

terms.text: A white spends at least 6 months in oak and 18 months in all, and a red at least 6 months in oak and 24 months in all.
A white needs 6 months in oak and 24 months in all, and a red 12 months in oak and 36 months in all. A sparkling wine may also be called Reserva after at least 15 months from tirage to disgorging.
A white needs 6 months in oak and 48 months in all, and a red 24 months in oak and 60 months in all.
A wine from a masía (a Catalan farmhouse) documented before 1900, from organic vines at least ten years old within 2 km of the farmhouse. Its grape yields are 15% below the general limit.

The higher step of Vino de Mas: vines at least 25 years old, only the local varieties the rules list, such as Xarel·lo or Ull de Llebre, and at least ten years of acclaim in national or international publications.
A wine with its vintage on the label, bottled between October of the harvest year and the following January.
A wine with its vintage on the label, bottled in the same year as its harvest.
The wine spent time in oak containers of at most 600 litres. The label must say for how many months or years.
The wine spent time in wooden containers of at most 600 litres. The label must say for how many months or years.
The wine fermented in those same wooden containers. The time in them need not be given.
An ancestral-method sparkling wine aged at least 4 years from tirage under a cork, sold without disgorging.
